Case study · clinical quality and risk management

What if every study team saw the same risks, the same way?

Designing one platform that unifies risk assessment, surveillance, a standard risk library and a metric hub for one of the Fortune 500 clients in pharma.

RoleProduct Designer
TeamProduct manager, product owner, 3 designers, BAs, frontend and backend developers, QA
Timeline1 year 8 months, 3 major releases
ToolsFigma, Miro, JIRA, shared design system

Context. Clinical studies must protect participants and produce reliable data. Risk-based quality management (RBQM) helps study teams focus on the risks that matter most: they identify Critical to Quality (CtQ) factors, assess the risks around them, set controls and watch Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) as the study runs.

The problem

Risk lived in many tools, and none of them agreed.

Risk assessments, indicators, reference lists and approvals sat in separate systems. Every study team rebuilt the same logic its own way, so the same risk was named and scored differently from study to study. The COE could not easily show Health Authorities a systematic approach.

What teams couldn't answer

  • "Which version of this risk is the approved one?"
  • "Is the same risk scored the same way in every study?"
  • "Who signed off this indicator, and when?"
How might we give study teams and the COE one connected place to assess, monitor and govern risk?
The challenge

The work spanned several modules and two audiences, with no direct access to end users.

The opportunity

One governed library that every module draws on, so teams can trust what they see.

UX goals

Make fragmented risk work visible, consistent and governed.

Consolidate

One platform instead of many tools and hand-offs.

Speed up

A faster path from study start to approved assessment.

Standardise

Reuse approved risks, controls and metrics.

Govern

Every metric versioned and approved by the Librarian.

Make state clear

Draft, approved, rejected and discarded are always visible.

My role and constraints

  • Worked with BAs, the product manager and product owner day to day, then handed designs to developers and QA.
  • Constraint: no direct access to users. The BAs ran workshops for our team, so they were our source of requirements.
  • Constraint: a regulated domain, so approvals and version history had to be built in.
  • Constraint: phased delivery across three releases, so patterns had to be reusable.

User base and personas

Three archetypes, built from what the BAs told us.

We had no direct user access, so we built proto-personas from the BA workshops and used empathy mapping to test them.

Program Steward

RBQM COE member

Wants consistent RBQM across studies and proof for Health Authorities.

Struggles with no single view and inconsistent risk language.

Needs visibility, standard definitions and an audit trail.

Study Risk Owner

Clinical study team member

Wants a sound risk assessment, fast.

Struggles with rebuilding standard risks and switching tools.

Needs smart suggestions and less manual entry.

Librarian

Governance approver

Wants an accurate, versioned library and metrics.

Struggles with unclear history and reviewing without context.

Needs a clear queue, full details in one view, simple approve and reject.

Process

Designing second-hand, carefully.

01
Absorb

The client ran workshops for the BA team, and the BAs ran workshops for ours. We learned the RBQM vocabulary before designing anything.

02
Synthesize

Affinity mapping, empathy maps, proto-personas and journey maps turned BA input into design inputs.

03
Design

Flows, wireframes and high-fidelity screens in the shared design system, with reusable table, status and graph patterns.

04
Review and release

Reviews with BAs, PM, PO and developers. Minor changes went into the current release, and major ones moved to the next.

Journey maps: before and after

Key decisions

What we chose, and why.

One governed library as the foundation

Considered
Each module keeping its own lists of risks and controls.
Chose
A single searchable library of standard risks, controls, critical data and processes that every module draws on.
Because
Consistency had to come before features.

Suggested risks instead of a blank page

Considered
Leaving teams to search the library themselves.
Chose
Automated suggestions tailored to each study, so teams spend their time on study-specific risks.
Because
Rebuilding standard risks each time drained the team's time.

Limits drawn as graphs in the Metric Hub

Considered
Entering upper and lower limits as plain fields.
Chose
Metrics built from KRIs with versioned names, parameter values, an SQL section, and limits drawn on a graph.
Because
Seeing a threshold against the data catches mistakes before submission.

Visible status in Work Bench

Considered
Showing only the latest version of each metric.
Chose
A table of every metric with version details and a clear status: draft, approved, rejected or discarded.
Because
In a regulated domain, state and history are part of the experience.

A decision queue for the Librarian

Considered
Opening each metric record to review it.
Chose
My Tasks shows every detail in one table, with an approve or reject button in the last column.
Because
A Librarian can decide quickly and with full context.

Flows and screens

The platform, end to end.

Outcome

What shipped, and what changed.

-80%Tools per risk assessment (5 to 1)
-60%Time to complete a risk assessment (10 hrs to 4 hrs)
+55 ptsAssessments built from library items (20% to 75%)
-67%Metric approval turnaround (6 days to 2 days)
-63%Change requests per release (24 to 9)
+60 ptsConsistency of risk language (30% to 90%)
Delivered

Across 3 major releases: Risk Assessment and the Library first, then Surveillance and the Metric Hub.

Replaced

A patchwork of disconnected tools with one governed platform.

Scoped next

Portfolio Insights, a learning loop from each study, and predictive risk signals.

Reflection

In regulated domains, governance is part of the experience: versions, statuses and approvals needed as much care as the main screens. A shared library did more for consistency than any single screen. And designing second-hand works when you cross-check early and bring open questions back to the BAs.
